content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has been working to eliminate kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) as a public health problem in the South-East Asia Region, where the disease is predominantly endemic in Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, with sporadic cases reported in Bhutan and Thailand. In 2005, a regional initiative was launched to reduce the incidence of kala-azar to less than 1 case per 10,000 population at the sub-district level in Bangladesh and India, and at the district level in Nepal. Nepal has maintained this target since 2014, and other endemic countries are nearing the goal. To validate the elimination of kala-azar as a public health problem, a formal process has been outlined. This includes defining specific criteria for validation, documenting progress, and ensuring sustained elimination. The validation process involves assessing whether the annual incidence rate of kala-azar remains below 1 case per 10,000 population for at least three consecutive years in the implementation units (sub-districts, blocks, or districts). Additionally, the process emphasizes the importance of monitoring and addressing post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), which can act as a reservoir for the disease. The elimination initiative has led to significant reductions in kala-azar cases across the region. For example, in India, cases decreased from 44,533 in 2007 to 9,241 in 2014. Similarly, Bangladesh saw a reduction from 9,370 cases in 2006 to 1,038 in 2014, and Nepal from 1,564 cases in 2005 to 280 in 2014. By 2014, Nepal had achieved the elimination target in all endemic districts, while 96% of endemic sub-districts in Bangladesh and 74% of endemic blocks in India had reached the target. The initiative employs several strategies, including early diagnosis and complete treatment, integrated vector management, effective disease and vector surveillance, social mobilization, and operational research. Active case detection methods, such as house-to-house visits, health camps, and index case-based approaches, are used to identify new cases of kala-azar and PKDL. Passive case detection, where patients self-report to health facilities, is also utilized. Challenges remain, including underreporting of cases, variability in surveillance systems, and the need for standardized active case-finding strategies. The WHO emphasizes the importance of robust epidemiological surveillance, cross-border coordination, and ensuring access to diagnosis and treatment. Countries are encouraged to document their progress, including the proportion of unreported cases, and to establish mechanisms for sustained elimination. The validation process involves an independent expert team reviewing country reports, visiting endemic areas, and assessing the reliability of data. If the team is satisfied that elimination has been achieved, monitoring will continue through annual reports and periodic joint missions. The ultimate goal is to maintain the elimination of kala-azar as a public health problem on a permanent basis.
